summary: DNSSEC signatures can use different algorithms. This document specifies how validating resolvers can signal to a server which digital signature and hash algorithms they support. This lets zone administrators learn when new algorithms are supported widely enough to start using them.

eli5.summary: A resolver tells a server which secret-code styles it understands, so the server knows when it is safe to switch to a newer style.

questions: how do dns resolvers signal supported dnssec algorithms
what are dau dhu and n3u
how do i know when to roll a dnssec algorithm
subtitle: How a DNSSEC validating resolver tells servers which signature and hash algorithms it understands.

tldr.problem: Zone administrators who want to retire an old DNSSEC algorithm and switch to a new one have no way to know whether enough clients can validate the new algorithm.
tldr.mechanism: Validating resolvers add three optional EDNS0 options (DAU, DHU and N3U) to their queries, each listing the signature, DS hash or NSEC3 hash algorithm codes they support.
tldr.outcome: Servers only observe the lists and must not change their answers because of them, so administrators can measure uptake, possibly over years, before completing an algorithm rollover.

facts.label: Estimated size of all three options

today: RFC 6975 is a Proposed Standard (Standards Track) from July 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is built on the EDNS0 mechanism from RFC 6891.

sections.title: Why Algorithm Signaling Exists
sections.content:
DNSSEC protects DNS data with digital signatures. Each RRSIG record carries an algorithm code number that matches a DNSKEY record, and DS and NSEC3 records use hash algorithms that also have code numbers. All three sets of codes live in separate IANA registries.

When a zone moves to a new algorithm, the administrator needs to know when it is safe to stop signing with the superseded one. RFC 6975 provides a way for a client query to say which algorithms the client implements. The RFC states that three new EDNS0 options are all OPTIONAL to implement and use.

The RFC is explicit about what it does not do: it adds no new process for introducing DNSSEC algorithms and does not say which algorithms should be mandatory or recommended.
sections.eli5: When a school wants to switch to a new secret code, it first needs to know how many students can already read it. This RFC gives the students a way to say so.

sections.title: The DAU, DHU and N3U Options
sections.content:
The three options travel in the RDATA of the EDNS0 OPT pseudo-record. They can be used independently, may appear in any order, and each option code may appear only once in an OPT record.

  • DAU (DNSSEC Algorithm Understood), option code 5, lists signing algorithms.
  • DHU (DS Hash Understood), option code 6, lists DS record hash algorithms.
  • N3U (NSEC3 Hash Understood), option code 7, lists NSEC3 hash algorithms.

Each option holds an OPTION-CODE, a LIST-LENGTH in octets, and a list of algorithm codes, one octet per code. The order of the codes can be arbitrary and MUST NOT be used to infer preference.

With all three options present, the RFC estimates they are likely to take 22 to 32 octets.
sections.eli5: Three little notes can be clipped to a question: one for signature styles, one for one kind of fingerprint, and one for another kind. Each note is just a list of numbers, and the order does not mean favorite.

sections.title: What Clients and Resolvers Do
sections.content:
A validating resolver sets the DAU, DHU and/or N3U option in the query. It MUST also set the DNSSEC OK (DO) bit. A validating stub resolver SHOULD include the options, while a non-validating stub resolver MUST NOT.

A client is not obliged to list every algorithm it implements. The RFC sees no compelling reason to list PRIVATEDNS (253) or PRIVATEOID (254), since those cover a wide range of algorithms and are likely not useful to a server. A client MUST NOT include RESERVED codes.

A validating recursive resolver MUST send the union of the stub's list and its own list on outgoing iterative queries. In the RFC's example, a resolver list of (3, 5, 7) and a stub list of (7, 8) give (3, 5, 7, 8). It MUST NOT set the options in the final response to the stub. A non-validating recursive resolver MUST copy the options it sees, because they express the wishes of the downstream validator. Intermediate DNS-aware proxies are RECOMMENDED to behave like a comparable recursive resolver.

The options only belong in queries, so a client that sees them in a response MUST ignore them.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle who passes questions along should combine the lists from everyone behind it. A helper who cannot check codes at all just copies the list it was handed.

sections.title: What Servers Must and Must Not Do
sections.content:
When an authoritative server sees the options, it follows the normal algorithm for answering. The options MUST NOT trigger any special processing, such as filtering RRSIG records out of responses.

If the options are present but the DO bit is not set, the server does no DNSSEC processing, which includes recording the options. If an option contains RESERVED values, the server MAY ignore recording them. Authoritative servers MUST NOT set the options on any response.
sections.eli5: The server just reads the note and writes the numbers in its notebook. It must not change its answer because of the note.

sections.title: Measuring Uptake Before a Rollover
sections.content:
Administrators planning an algorithm rollover should monitor DNS query traffic and record the number of queries, whether an OPT record was present, and the DAU, DHU and N3U values. How to capture and measure that traffic is outside the scope of the RFC.

The data can help set milestone dates for a rollover. To keep disruption small, administrators should wait until a large majority of clients signal that they recognize the new algorithm, which may take years rather than months. Clients that do not implement the options are likely older implementations that would not implement a newly deployed algorithm either.
sections.eli5: Count how many people say they can read the new code. Wait until almost everyone can, even if that takes a long time.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The signals are optional and are not a discussion of which algorithm is better. The RFC notes one privacy-style risk: an eavesdropper or server could infer which validator a client uses from the presence of the options and the algorithm list. That leak is not very useful alone, but it could narrow down possible implementations, one of which might have a known vulnerability.

IANA allocated option codes 5, 6 and 7 for DAU, DHU and N3U in the DNS EDNS0 Option Codes (OPT) registry, with status standard. The existing algorithm registries are not changed.
sections.eli5: The list of codes you can read might hint at which brand of decoder you own. That is a small risk, but someone could use it to guess.
